name: Babylon
info: Babylon was an ancient city on the lower Euphrates in southern Mesopotamia, near modern Hillah in Iraq. It was the capital of two Babylonian empires and was last inhabited, as a small village, in the 11th century CE.

facts.founded: First mentioned in the reign of the Akkadian king Shar-Kali-Sharri (2217 to 2193 BCE) as a town of the Akkadian Empire; classical writers gave foundation dates in the 23rd century BCE that cuneiform records do not confirm
facts.where: On the lower Euphrates in southern Mesopotamia, near the modern city of Hillah in Iraq, about 85 kilometres south of Baghdad
facts.known: The Code of Hammurabi; the Old and Neo-Babylonian empires; Esagila and the ziggurat Etemenanki; the Ishtar Gate; the Hanging Gardens, whose existence is disputed; the exile of the Jews in the Hebrew Bible; the Tower of Babel; Babylonian astronomy
facts.today: The site is a ruin field near Hillah in Iraq, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019.

t: Babylon was a small town of the Akkadian Empire until Hammurabi, who ruled from 1792 to 1750 BCE, made it the capital of a kingdom that covered southern Mesopotamia.
It was destroyed by Sennacherib in 689 BCE and rebuilt, became the capital of the Neo-Babylonian Empire from 626 to 539 BCE, and then served as a capital of the Achaemenid Empire.
After the Hellenistic period it declined under Parthian, Sasanian and Muslim rule, and the last known habitation, a small village, dates from the 11th century CE.
dyk: Babylon has been estimated to have been the largest city in the world c. 1770 to c. 1670 BCE and again c. 612 to c. 320 BCE, and perhaps the first city to reach a population above 200,000.
ev: A year name of Shar-Kali-Sharri records the founding of temples in Babylon, its earliest reasonably firm mention
Hammurabi becomes king and builds Babylon into the capital of southern Mesopotamia
The city is thought to have been sacked by the Hittite king Mursili I
Sennacherib of Assyria destroys the city
Cyrus the Great takes Babylon and ends the Neo-Babylonian Empire
Alexander the Great enters Babylon after the Battle of Gaugamela
Robert Koldewey begins the first scientific excavations
UNESCO inscribes Babylon as a World Heritage Site

sections.origins:
Babylon stood on the lower Euphrates, in what is now the area of Hillah in Iraq. The name appears in Akkadian as Bābilim, "gate of the god(s)", but this reading is increasingly viewed as a Semitic folk etymology for an unknown original name, which I. J. Gelb thought was Babilla. The earliest reasonably firm mention is one of the year names of Shar-Kali-Sharri (2217 to 2193 BCE), which records the founding of temples of Annunitum and Ilaba in the city. Babylon was then a religious and cultural centre but a town of the Akkadian Empire, not an independent state, and it was ruled by a governor, an ensi. It was later included in the realm of the Third Dynasty of Ur, whose records name an ensi there.

Classical writers dated the founding much earlier. Ctesias, quoted by Diodorus Siculus, placed it in 2286 BCE under a first king, Belus; Berossus, according to Pliny, implies 2243 BCE; and Stephanus of Byzantium implies 2231 BCE. All fall in the 23rd century BCE, but no cuneiform records correspond to them. The Weidner Chronicle says that Sargon of Akkad built Babylon "in front of Akkad", though Van de Mieroop suggested that the Assyrian king Sargon II is meant. In the Hebrew Bible, Genesis 10:10 says that Babel was founded by Nimrod with Uruk and Akkad. A fragmentary votive inscription of about 2700 BCE has been proposed to name Babylon, but the attribution is considered doubtful.
sections.growth:
Babylon was at first a minor city-state with little territory, overshadowed by Elam, Isin and Larsa. Under Hammurabi (r. 1792 to 1750 BCE) it became the capital of a kingdom that took in the cities of southern Mesopotamia, and from his time the region was called Babylonia. Babylon supplanted Nippur and Eridu as the main religious centre of the south. It has been estimated that Babylon was the largest city in the world c. 1770 to c. 1670 BCE, and again c. 612 to c. 320 BCE, and perhaps the first to exceed 200,000 people. The whole site covers about 1,000 hectares, with about 450 hectares inside the walls.

The greatest rebuilding came after Nabopolassar freed Babylon from Assyria and the city became the capital of the Neo-Babylonian Empire. His son Nebuchadnezzar II ordered the reconstruction of the imperial grounds, including the ziggurat Etemenanki, and built the Ishtar Gate, the most prominent of eight gates. Before his reign construction was mainly of unbaked brick; his reign saw heavy use of baked brick. The Hanging Gardens, said to have been built for his homesick wife Amytis, were counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, but they are not mentioned in any surviving Babylonian text. Robert Koldewey thought he had found their foundations, many historians disagree about the location, and Stephanie Dalley has argued that they stood near Nineveh.
sections.rulers:
According to a Babylonian king list, Amorite rule began in the 19th or 18th century BCE with Sumu-abum, and Sumu-la-El is usually given as the first of the First Babylonian dynasty. After Hammurabi the empire weakened under his son Samsu-iluna. The city is thought to have been sacked by the Hittite king Mursili I in 1595 BCE, in the reign of Samsu-Ditana, the last ruler of the dynasty. The Kassites then took power, renamed the city Karduniash and held it for 435 years, until 1160 BCE; it later paid tribute to Egypt and fell under Assyrian and Elamite pressure. From 911 BCE Babylonia was under constant Assyrian domination or direct control. Nabopolassar escaped Assyrian rule and, with his allies, destroyed the Assyrian Empire between 626 and 609 BCE, so that Babylon became the capital of the Neo-Babylonian or Chaldean Empire.

In 539 BCE the empire fell to Cyrus the Great of Persia, and Babylon became the capital of the 9th satrapy of the Achaemenid Empire. Native Babylonian kings briefly regained independence in 522, 521 and 482 BCE, but these revolts were put down. Alexander the Great entered in October 331 BCE after defeating Darius III at Gaugamela, and died in 323 BCE in Nebuchadnezzar's palace. Babylon then lay within the Seleucid Empire, and later belonged to the Parthian and Sasanian empires for nine centuries. Trajan took it briefly in 116 CE, but Hadrian gave up the conquests east of the Euphrates. In the mid 7th century the Muslim empire took Mesopotamia and dissolved Babylon as a province.
sections.life:
Babylon was the main cultural and political centre of the Akkadian-speaking region of Babylonia. The Euphrates, which has shifted slightly since ancient times, ran through the city, and its mounds mark the main buildings: Esagila, the temple of Marduk with shrines of Ea and Nabu, and Etemenanki on the Kasr mound. Old Babylonian texts often treat the sun god Shamash as a supreme deity and Marduk as his son; Marduk was later raised to a higher status. Under the Achaemenids Babylonian astronomy and mathematics were revitalised and scholars completed maps of constellations, though by the reign of Darius III over-taxation and war had led to a decay of the main shrines and canals.

Herodotus described a moat, an enormously tall and broad wall cemented with bitumen and a hundred gates, and customs of the Babylonians. After Archibald Sayce's pronouncement in 1883 his account was largely taken as Greek folklore, though Dalley and others have recently suggested taking it seriously. Ctesias, Quintus Curtius Rufus, Strabo and Cleitarchus also described the city, with variable accuracy. According to the Hebrew Bible, Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Solomon's Temple and exiled the Jews to Babylon, and the Babylonian Chronicles record the defeat. Under Parthian and Sasanian rule the people spoke varieties of Aramaic and still called their land Babylon; the Babylonian Talmud, the Mandaean religion, the East Syrian rite and Manichaeism come from this culture, and Babylon was the seat of a bishop of the Church of the East.
sections.crises:
Sennacherib of Assyria, facing continual revolt in Babylonia, destroyed the city completely in 689 BCE: its walls, temples and palaces were razed and the rubble was thrown into the Arakhtu. The destruction shocked many, and his murder by two of his sons was considered an act of atonement. His successor Esarhaddon rebuilt the city. In 652 BCE Shamash-shum-ukin started a civil war against his brother Ashurbanipal, and Babylon was besieged and starved into surrender. In 539 BCE, according to the account elaborated by Herodotus, the Persians diverted the Euphrates during a feast and entered along the river bed while most Babylonians in the centre did not know of the breach. Alexander is said to have demolished Etemenanki in 331 BCE, and most of its remains were heaped on the Homera mound.

After the Hellenistic period Babylon declined. Ibn Hawqal in the 10th century and al-Qazwini in the 13th describe a small village, and medieval Arabic writings say that bricks were taken from the site to build cities from Baghdad to Basra. Large-scale mining of baked bricks, mostly from the time of Nebuchadnezzar II, continued in the 19th century. Isaiah 13:19 and Jeremiah 50 say that Babylon would never be inhabited, but coins from the Parthian, Sasanian and Arabic periods show continuous settlement. The last known habitation dates from the 11th century CE, when the place was called the "small village of Babel".
sections.legacy:
For centuries European travellers could not find the city, and some took Fallujah for it, while others called Baghdad Babylon or New Babylon. Claudius Rich excavated in 1811 to 1812 and 1817, and Fulgence Fresnel, Julius Oppert and Felix Thomas in 1852 to 1854; much of their work was lost when a transport ship and rafts sank on the Tigris in May 1855. Hormuzd Rassam dug for the British Museum from 1879 to 1882, and his methods damaged the archaeological context. Robert Koldewey's German team made the first scientific excavations, daily from 1899 to 1917, concentrating on the temple of Marduk, the Processional Way and the city wall, and pieces of the Ishtar Gate went to Berlin, where it was reconstructed in the Pergamon Museum. Most tablets from modern excavations remain unpublished.

In 1978 the Ba'athist government of Iraq under Saddam Hussein began the Archaeological Restoration of Babylon Project, rebuilding features such as the Southern Palace on the ruins, with bricks bearing his name. After the invasion of 2003 US forces built Camp Alpha on the ruins, and John Curtis of the British Museum reported damage to the Ishtar Gate, crushed brick pavements, and trenches cut into ancient deposits. The site was handed to the Iraqi Ministry of Culture in 2005, reopened to visitors in 2009 and inscribed by UNESCO in 2019. Villages lie within the ancient outer walls, and building is encroaching on the ruins.

summary: Babylon was a city on the lower Euphrates that rose under Hammurabi and again under Nebuchadnezzar II, and served later empires as a regional capital. It declined from the Hellenistic period and was a village by the 11th century CE. Its ruins near Hillah are a World Heritage Site.
references: Stephanie Dalley, The City of Babylon: A History c. 2000 BC – AD 116 (Cambridge University Press, 2021)
Paul-Alain Beaulieu, A History of Babylon, 2200 BC - AD 75 (Wiley-Blackwell, 2018)
Karen Radner, A Short History of Babylon (Bloomsbury Academic, 2020)
Olof Pedersén, Babylon: The Great City (Zaphon, 2021)
notes: Dates: start -2217 is the first year of Shar-Kali-Sharri's reign as the article gives it (2217 to 2193 BCE), the earliest reasonably firm mention; the article also notes a doubtful votive inscription c. 2700 BCE and classical foundation dates in the 23rd century BCE. end 1050 is my midpoint for 'the last known habitation ... from the 11th century AD'; the article gives no year.
Nebuchadnezzar II's reign is given as 605 to 562 BCE in the archaeology section and 604 to 561 BCE in the history section; I gave no reign years for him.
Kassite rule: 'until 1160 BC' in the first mention, but 'by 1155 BC ... the Kassites were deposed' in the next paragraph; I used 1160 only.
Area: 'about 900 ha' (the first city above 200,000) against 'about 1,000 hectares' for the site and 450 inside the walls; I gave only the latter two and the 200,000 hedge separately.
Muslim period: the article calls the end 'dissolved as a province' in the mid 7th century and the last habitation the 11th century; 'until after AD 650' for Parthian and Sasanian rule.
The Etemenanki demolition by Alexander is from the article's description of the Homera mound; I wrote 'is said to have'. The article gives Esagila's mound as Amran Ibn Ali.

The Muslim-period 'Dungeon of Daniel' and the shrine of Amran ibn Ali, Cultural importance (Rastafari, fiction) and the Biblical narrative apart from Genesis 10:10, Isaiah 13:19 and Jeremiah 50, were left out; the Tower of Babel is in 'known' only.

The ev line for 1792 BCE: the article says Hammurabi 'r. 1792 to 1750'; 'builds Babylon into the capital' is the article's wording in substance. The 1595 BCE sack is hedged in the article ('is thought to have been').

Wanted but not found: any figure for the population at the Neo-Babylonian peak beyond the 200,000 estimate; the year Babylon was last a capital under the Seleucids; the cause of the village's final abandonment; the damage figures for 2003 beyond the Curtis quotation.
